newsitem.title: UK: Major comfortably wins latest parliamentary test.
newsitem.headline: Major comfortably wins latest parliamentary test.

text.p: British Prime Minister John Major comfortably won the first important vote in parliament since he lost his overall majority last month.
In a late-night Tuesday vote on the finance bill implementing the 1997/1998 budget, the government defeated a hostile amendment put down by the main opposition Labour party by 322 votes to 287.

The outcome of the vote had never been seriously in doubt, but the margin of victory will be a boost to Major, who wants to delay Britain's general election until May to give more time for the strong economy to revive his Conservative party's fortunes.
"I am prepared to play it long, yes. Of course I am prepared to play it long," he told reporters earlier in Lahore, Pakistan, who asked him about the timing of the election.
Major left Pakistan more than an hour early so he could be sure of getting back to London in time to vote.

With 323 Conservatives equally matched in the lower House of Commons by 323 members of opposition parties, Major could not afford to risk missing the vote -- especially because Labour has vowed to mount parliamentary ambushes to try to wear out the government's nerves before polling day.

In the event, however, Major sailed home in part because the nine Ulster Unionist members of parliament, representing Northern Ireland's largest political party, decided not to vote against the government.
But Ulster Unionist leader David Trimble warned Major his party would fight plans to double Britain's airport departure tax when the budget legislation is scrutinised in committee.

Despite that threat, Labour strategists admit it will be difficult for them to force Major into an early election before a date of his choosing -- May 1 is thought to be his preferred option, while May 22 is the last legally possible date.

"This is not going to be a simple matter of a knock-out punch. It is a metter of keeping the pressure on and using the quite clearly disintegrating morale on the Conservative benches to further undermine confidence," Labour's chief business manager, Donald Dewar, told BBC television.

Labour, which has been in opposition since 1979, leads the Conservatives in opinion polls by some 20 percentage points, but Major performs best when his back is against the wall -- as he did in coming from behind to win the 1992 election.
"I like elections. I'm raring to go," he told reporters on his plane back from Pakistan on Tuesday.
